No. A 15% rise in CPU Latency with unchanged CPU Ready and Co-Stop is not evidence of CPU scheduling contention.

CPU Latency is the wall-clock time from when a vCPU is runnable to when it actually executes on physical hardware. It includes scheduler wait time plus non-scheduler delays such as power management wake latency, VM exits, and hypervisor overhead.

CPU Ready is time a vCPU is ready to run but is not scheduled by the hypervisor. Co-Stop is time vCPUs of a multi-vCPU VM are waiting for each other. Both are unchanged, so the hypervisor scheduling queue and SMP synchronization have not worsened.

A host BIOS power policy change, e.g. Performance -> Balanced/Power Save, increases C-state residency and P-state transitions. The physical cores take longer to wake and ramp frequency when dispatched. That adds to CPU Latency but does not increase CPU Ready because once the core is available the scheduler dispatches promptly. This is power-management latency, not contention.

Whether this is a performance problem cannot be settled from a relative 15% change alone. It depends on absolute latency and workload sensitivity.

No. Adding a seventh host will not clear the red state. The red is a reservation hierarchy inconsistency, not a capacity shortage.

The cluster has 480 GHz capacity and <40% usage. The problem is inside the Prod pool.

Prod at cluster root is 100 GHz Fixed. Its children are Prod-DB 70 GHz Expandable and Prod-App 45 GHz Expandable. The children demand 115 GHz of expandable reservation inside a parent that is guaranteed only 100 GHz Fixed.

With a Fixed parent the parent’s reservation is a hard guarantee from the cluster. The children’s expandable reservations can be satisfied only from that 100 GHz. Sum of children > parent is an overcommit of reservation within the pool. vSphere marks the pool red with “reservation exceeds parent reservation / insufficient resources” and DRS will warn. Capacity is irrelevant.

Risk to running VMs: No immediate power off. Under contention the effective reservation available to the Prod-DB and Prod-App trees is capped at the 100 GHz guaranteed to Prod, so the 115 GHz of expandable demand is rationed. VMs can see higher CPU Ready/latency, throttling and DRS anti-affinity issues when load rises. HA will still work but the reservation guarantee you thought you had is not real.

Fix: Reconcile the hierarchy. Either
* raise Prod’s Fixed reservation to >= sum of children, e.g. 115 GHz Fixed or more, or
* lower Prod-DB + Prod-App reservations to <= 100 GHz, or
* change Prod reservation type from Fixed to Expandable if you want the children to be able to borrow beyond 100 GHz.

Check next: vSphere Client > Alarms for ResourcePool reservation warnings, Monitor > Resources for effective reservations, and the change history that edited the reservations during the failover. Revert or correct the reservation edit before adding hardware.

Adding 8 more vCPUs will not help and will likely hurt. Total CPU usage is 16% and CPU Ready is 0.4%. The problem is interrupt/DPC affinity, not aggregate CPU. More vCPUs increase scheduling cost and will not move the DPC work off CPU0.

* Verify VMXNET3 RSS / queues. In the VM advanced adapter settings set Number of Receive Queues and Number of Transmit Queues to match vCPU count, e.g. 8, and ensure the VMXNET3 driver is current with VMware Tools. In Windows confirm RSS is enabled: Get-NetAdapterRss and Get-NetAdapterRssStats.

No. Windows In Use and VM Consumed measure different layers and different concepts, so they do not map and their patterns will diverge.

Mechanism and reason:
Guest OS and VM memory metrics do not map. Neither the VMkernel nor the Guest OS has full visibility into the other. ESXi sees a guest physical page only when it is first touched, via an EPT/RVI fault in the second-level page tables. Freeing, reusing and caching inside the Guest OS are ordinary guest memory writes that never reach ESXi. The two layers manage memory independently.

Consumed is an ESXi view of ESXi pages that have been active for the VM. Shared pages count once, ballooned and swapped VM pages have no ESXi page here, and Consumed can hold a lot of guest cache. It does not exist in Windows.

Windows In Use is a Guest OS classification. Windows compresses In Use pages even with plenty free, and the Guest OS free list is invisible to ESXi. When the guest frees a page it only updates its own free list; the hypervisor mapping stays in place, so Consumed stays high after Guest OS In Use drops. VMware Tools is the only channel for ESXi to ask the guest about memory, via the balloon driver.

What to check next:
Use Guest OS metrics for Guest OS health, e.g. Free memory and page-out rate, and VM metrics for hypervisor health, e.g. Active/Consumed. Monitor both layers in the same time window; do not equate In Use with Consumed.

Admission control fails on reservation, not on used memory. Host Consumed ~30% is usage and is irrelevant to power-on.

Admission control checks that all reservations can still be guaranteed. A reservation is a guarantee and cannot be overcommitted. It compares the VM’s reservation with the unreserved capacity of the host. Per-VM overhead memory counts as reserved on top of the memory reservation.

You have 512 GB total. Reservation available = 481 GB unreserved, so ~31 GB is already reserved by powered-on VMs. The test VM is configured with Reserve all guest memory = 480 GB reserved.

Required for admission = 480 GB reservation + per-VM overhead memory. That is > 481 GB unreserved, so power-on is refused with Insufficient memory resources. Host Consumed ≈ 30% ≈ 153 GB is actual use, including ESXi itself, and admission control never checks usage. A host at 10% usage can still refuse a VM if its capacity is already reserved.

What to change:
* Remove the reservation. Uncheck Reserve all guest memory. Then admission only needs to fit the VM overhead, not 480 GB, and the VM will power on and take memory on demand. Memory reservation is sticky and only effective once the VM has touched the pages.
* Or reduce the VM’s configured memory / reservation so reservation + overhead ≤ 481 GB unreserved.
* Or power off / move VMs to free existing reservations.

Mechanism for the spikes
With BIOS OS Controlled and C-states enabled, ESXi Balanced uses Use C States = 1 and Use P States = 1. That is full dynamic range: cores drop below base to save power, sleep when idle, and scale up to Turbo under load.

C-states are deeper = less power, longer time to start running again. ESXi predicts idle duration and picks the C-state to enter. C1 is shallow, return instantaneous. C2+ stops the external bus clock and deeper, flushes caches etc. After a quiet period the market-data VM’s cores are in a deep C-state. The first messages after idle require a C-state exit, which is the few-hundred-microsecond latency you see. Power management features in newer server hardware can increase network latency. The source prefers Maximum performance for latency-sensitive workloads.

Guest sees one vNUMA node because vNUMA topology is fixed at first power-on and persists across migrations.

vNUMA topology is set at first power-on. It is based partly on the NUMA topology of the host. The topology does not change unless the VM vCPU count changes. If a vNUMA VM moves to a host with a different NUMA topology, its vNUMA topology may no longer suit the host. The result can be reduced performance.

First power-on was on a new host: 2 sockets, 32 cores per socket, 1 NUMA node per socket. 20 vCPUs ≤ 32 cores per node and 160 GB < 512 GB per socket, so vNUMA created one vNUMA node for the VM. After DRS moved the VM to an old host, the vNUMA topology was not recreated. The guest therefore still sees one node.
